# THEORYs with `tags` `emotion-and-affect`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Emotion and affect** — emotions, feelings and affect — what they are, their bodily and neural basis (including the homeostatic and interoceptive states feelings are said to report), their role in decision, memory and behaviour, and whether they ground consciousness (group: philosophy; ADR-014).

| [THEORY-045](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-045.md) v3 | Felt affect is experience of the regulatory state | Barrett (2017), [LIT-542](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-542.md), and Damasio & Carvalho (2013), [LIT-388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-388.md), are two independent accounts that agree on a base layer. What is felt as affect (valence and arousal for Barrett, feeling for Damasio) is the body's regulatory state. Its valence is that state's value for the organism, and it is present in hunger, pain and well-being as much as in emotion. They disagree about what the experience is of. For Barrett it is the brain's allostatic prediction of the body, issued from agranular limbic cortex. For Damasio it is a topographic map of the body's state, built in the upper brainstem, and their paper makes no use of prediction. Seth ([LIT-135](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-135.md)) builds on the same base but makes his claim about consciousness, not about affect. Friston ([LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md)) supports neither. Proposed: both sources are theoretical syntheses, and neither tests the claim. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-050](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-050.md) | Psychological inflexibility is transdiagnostic | Hayes et al. ([LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)) model psychopathology as inflexibility: cognitive fusion supports experiential avoidance, which narrows behaviour. Barnes-Holmes et al. ([LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)) give the mechanism: once a word stands in derived relation to an event it can carry that event's aversive functions, so private events become worth avoiding. Kashdan and Rottenberg ([LIT-553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-553.md)) find inflexibility across depression and anxiety in cognitive, behavioural and physiological systems, and say its causal role is unknown. The evidence is correlational, small, mostly self-report and mostly from the model's authors, and the meta-analysis that would test it ([LIT-543](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-543.md)) is unread, so Proposed. It is compatible with the loop account of disorder, not a rival to it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-055](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-055.md) | Appraisal elicits emotion as action readiness | Frijda, Ridderinkhof & Rietveld (2014), [LIT-540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-540.md), Frijda's own late statement of the theory of The Emotions ([LIT-546](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-546.md), unread). An automatic appraisal of how an event bears on one's concerns elicits a state of action readiness: a motive to change one's relation to the object, with control precedence. Emotions differ by mode (hostility for anger, avoidance for fear), and "in the absence of concern pertinence … no emotion". It is the record's only read statement of an appraisal theory, because Lazarus ([LIT-550](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-550.md)) is unread. Both the elicitation claim and the claim that emotions differ by mode are argued, and neither is tested. The second is partly definitional within the theory. Rivals [THEORY-057](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-057.md): both accounts let instances vary and group them by function, but the appraisal account puts the unity in the agent's readiness and the constructionist account puts it in the perceiver's concept. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-056](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-056.md) v5 | Regulation is not separate from emotion generation | Frijda, Ridderinkhof & Rietveld (2014), [LIT-540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-540.md), deny "the exclusivity of emotion regulation processes". Appraising the consequences of an impulse raises a competing readiness, as when fear of retaliation holds back anger, so control is the interaction of motive states and not reason governing emotion. Barrett (2017), [LIT-542](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-542.md), reaches the second half from the opposite side of the emotion debate: automaticity and control are "different brain modes … not two battling brain systems", and she offers as a hypothesis that reappraisal works by the same predictions that construct emotion. Two rival theories of what an emotion is agree on this. Gross (1998), [LIT-554](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-554.md), poses the question and keeps the distinction. Proposed: argued from examples and from architecture, untested. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-057](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-057.md) | Emotion categories are not natural kinds | Barrett (2017), [LIT-542](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-542.md): degeneracy, population thinking, and a table of findings in which no region, network, pattern or neuron is consistent for an emotion category. From these she concludes that categories such as fear are populations of variable instances, grouped by a goal and constructed by categorization with a concept. She rejects basic-emotion and causal appraisal theories as positing a "Lockean essence". This is the record's only read statement of the view. The record's philosophy holdings sharpen it. Pernu ([LIT-147](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-147.md)) shows that many-to-one realisation at a fine grain does not rule out one variable at a coarser grain, so degeneracy alone does not carry the conclusion, and Table 1 has to. Searle ([LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md)) shows that Barrett's comparison with money is to observer-relative function, not to institutions. Rivals the appraisal account, [THEORY-055](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-055.md). Proposed: one theoretical paper, no independent test, and the reply unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-090](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-090.md) v2 | Basic affective consciousness is subcortical | Newen & Montemayor's ALARM theory (2025), [LIT-626](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-626.md): basic arousal, a sensitivity to pain, pleasure and other basic affect without focused attention, can be realised without cortex, by the upper brainstem and thalamus, and its function is to alarm the bodily agent when a homeostatic variable leaves its range, giving the signal "100% weight" through "rather rigid behavioural programmes without choices". Damasio & Carvalho (2013), [LIT-388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-388.md), supply the subcortical clause independently: feeling is generated in the upper brainstem and the insula is not needed. Both papers argue from cited evidence and offer no new data, and neither has a marker that tells a felt alarm from an unfelt one. The function clause rests on ALARM alone, and Veit's account rivals it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-093](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-093.md) v2 | Homeostatic feelings make contents conscious | Damasio & Damasio (2022), [LIT-628](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-628.md), an essay with no data, read only through a summarising fetch tool, so its wording is paraphrased here. Consciousness is the spontaneous identification of mind contents as belonging to one's own organism, and a continuous stream of homeostatic feelings, from hunger and pain to a faint feeling of existing, supplies it; the feelings are conscious in themselves and confer consciousness on exteroceptive images. They are hybrid because interoceptive axons are unmyelinated, partly non-synaptic and outside a systematic blood–brain barrier, so viscera and circulating molecules act on the neurons that map them. Damasio & Carvalho (2013), [LIT-388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-388.md), read in full, supply the upper-brainstem site of feeling and the unmyelinated-fibre proposal. Proposed: the identification is a definition, the mechanism an interpretation of anatomy, and the clinical evidence does not separate this account from its rivals. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-101](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-101.md) v2 | Consciousness began as hedonic valence | Veit's pathological complexity thesis, as he restates and defends it in his reply to commentators (2025), [LIT-105](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-105.md): consciousness originated as hedonic valence, "a common currency of sharing evaluative information across multiple control systems", which animals with many degrees of freedom need to solve the combinatorial trade-offs of action selection. Felt valence is identical with that currency, "not Cartesian but cybernetic". Motivational trade-offs are his criterion for consciousness. The source is a reply piece; the thesis is argued in a book the record has not read, and the mechanism is a sketch. ALARM ([THEORY-090](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-090.md)) rivals it on what the first consciousness did. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-123](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-123.md) v2 | Moods spread through groups by contagion | Barsade (2002), [LIT-706](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-706.md), read from the August 2001 manuscript, so every number is the manuscript's. Study 1 (94 undergraduates, 29 groups): a confederate randomly assigned to show pleasant or unpleasant mood moved members' self-reported mood by +.41 or −.26 (χ²(1) = 9.97), and blind video-coders rated members' mood 2.75 against 2.33 (χ²(1) = 10.30). Members who caught more pleasant mood were rated more cooperative, and at group level coder-rated contagion correlated with cooperativeness (r = .44) and against conflict (r = −.42). Study 2 (113 MBA students, 26 groups, no confederate): the ICC of members' mood rose from .00 to .24, and contagion correlated with members' ratings of cooperation (.49) and conflict (−.49). Members related how pleasantly they behaved to others' conduct but showed "absolutely no awareness" of mood bearing on their judged effectiveness. Valence and energy hypotheses failed or were marginal. Limits: one experiment, one actor, retrospective mood, correlational process effects. Promoted 2026-10-20 on what the manuscript measured (ADR-047 v3); the wider claim is THEORY-826. | Active |
| [THEORY-125](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-125.md) | Group emotion is possible, though none is shown | Huebner (2010), [LIT-702](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-702.md): a genuinely collective emotion is a state of a group that "could not be exhaustively characterized in terms of intentional states of individuals in aggregation". Fear requires danger detection, redeployment of attention, system-wide preparatory change and their coordination into one state with indicative content and imperative force; a distributed system can integrate routines that way. Some individual emotions are non-conscious, so a group's need not be felt, and emotion kinds are functional ("like vodka"), so lacking homologous mechanisms does not exclude groups. The paper establishes a possibility, not an instance: its worked case, the USS Palau crew, turns out to be "collective detection of danger in the absence of a fear response", and the replacement, the 2008 McCain–Palin campaign, is offered as "intuitively plausible" pending anthropological data. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-126](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-126.md) v2 | Collective emotion needs no group subject | von Scheve & Ismer (2013), [LIT-696](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-696.md), a conceptual synthesis with no data: collective emotion is "synchronous convergence in affective responding across individuals towards a specific event or object". Its minimal case is shared appraisal with no mutual awareness (drivers in one traffic jam). Mutual awareness and membership in a collective amplify it, and appraisals grounded in collective intentions give "We-mode" collective emotion, which they expect to differ in quality. Barsade (2002), [LIT-706](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-706.md), supplies the one measured instance: in 26 groups with no confederate, the intraclass correlation of members' mood rose from .00 to .24. The account posits no group subject and does not deny one. Proposed: the definition is stipulated, the routes beyond contagion are untested, and the We-mode clause is a hypothesis its authors say lacks evidence. | Proposed |

This sits uneasily with the "excess action" that Bencherki et al. ([LIT-1902](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1902.md)) have passing between individuation processes. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1462](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1462.md) v2 | Poverty stress may bias choice; no trap shown | Haushofer & Fehr (2014), [LIT-2152](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2152.md), read in [NOTE-1681](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1681.md): a Science Review. The first link has field causal support (18 of 25 causal studies; the Kenya cash-transfer trial); the second, which they call "the weakest link", has laboratory inductions only, with samples of 36 to 189 and acute rather than chronic stress. Active as a report of what the authors hold, that weakness included. It does not say that support raises effort or that a trap exists: no effort or labour response is measured, and income and psychological outcomes "show no strong signs of being nonlinear". | Active |
| [THEORY-1533](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1533.md) | Affect is felt change in capacity to act | The wide form of [THEORY-1282](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1282.md), kept when the twenty-seventh status review promoted that entry as a report ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md); [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md), kind 1): Massumi's account of affect taken as true, not as reported. He offers it as a proposition, after Spinoza and Deleuze, with no evidence, and refuses its use as a criterion; whether it picks out anything an account of emotion or appraisal does not is open. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1539](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1539.md) | Poverty's stress makes people present-biased | The thesis Haushofer and Fehr (2014), [LIT-2152](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2152.md), assert, split from [THEORY-1462](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1462.md) when the twenty-eighth status review promoted the report of their account ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md); [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1462](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1462.md) holds that they hold it; whether it is true outside the laboratory is this entry's question, under the condition [THEORY-1462](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1462.md) carried, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1592](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1592.md) v3 | Group identification yields group-based emotion | Smith and Mackie (2016), [LIT-1690](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1690.md), read in [NOTE-1285](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1285.md). A five-page review by the founders of intergroup emotions theory, with no new data. Four facts: the emotion follows the salient membership; members converge on a group norm; no personal involvement is needed; identification moderates, the highly identified sometimes reappraising to avoid guilt. Group-based emotions predict collective action and can be regulated. | Active |
| [THEORY-1631](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1631.md) | Lived immortality modes predict their consolation | Sturesteps (1992), [LIT-1689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1689.md), an ANU master's thesis skimmed in [NOTE-1312](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1312.md) in place of Lifton (1979, [LIT-1714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1714.md)). It tests Rank's three modes and Lifton's two added ones with vignettes rated as consolation, separating having a mode (availability) from accepting it. Cross-sectional; Rank's sex-difference and neuroticism hypotheses failed. The copy limits copying, so almost nothing is quoted. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2098](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2098.md) | Consciousness is affective, born in the brainstem | From the reading of [LIT-2891](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2891.md) in [NOTE-2186](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2186.md), a stand-in for [LIT-2916](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2916.md). Proposed until its promote_when is met. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2207](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2207.md) | Flow is higher at work, happiness at leisure | Rheinberg et al. (2007), [LIT-3071](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-3071.md), read in [NOTE-2297](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2297.md). One of the record's two read in-episode studies of flow and affect, both found by [LEAD-054](../../../record/leads.d/LEAD-054.md). Flow and happiness/satisfaction rated at each signal correlate r = .36 raw, .30 within-person, so some of flow's positivity is reported during the episode; it corroborates [CLAIM-441](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-441.md)'s premise that flow is reported as positive, against its third exit, weakly, since the correlation is pooled and flow is a continuous score. The sharp edge is the dissociation: goal-directedness lifts flow and not happiness. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2208](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2208.md) | Flow doesn't predict later valence | Engeser and Baumann (2014), [LIT-3070](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-3070.md), read in [NOTE-2298](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2298.md). The more direct of the record's two read in-episode studies of flow and affect, both found by [LEAD-054](../../../record/leads.d/LEAD-054.md). Within persons flow correlates .31 with valence and .59 with positive activation at the same signal, and does not raise valence at the next. It corroborates [CLAIM-441](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-441.md)'s premise that flow is positive during the episode, against the third exit that the positivity comes after it. The sharp edges: a continuous flow score with no enjoyment item, a two-hour lag, and a sample it appears to share with Rheinberg et al. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2236](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2236.md) | Expecting repeat choices weakens self-control | Khan and Dhar (2007), [LIT-3113](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-3113.md), read in [NOTE-2326](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2326.md) for [LEAD-078](../../../record/leads.d/LEAD-078.md). A recurring choice is a licence unless it is seen as a precedent: the vice share rises from 46.6-57.5% in isolation to 70-90% when the same choice is announced for next week, and falls to 53% when the chooser is told this choice is the best indicator of the next. It bears on [THEORY-067](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-067.md)'s first promotion condition, in part, and on [QUESTION-034](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-034.md)'s bargaining route. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2244](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2244.md) | Critical slowing precedes some relapses, weakly | Smit et al. (2025), [LIT-3125](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-3125.md), read from its preprint in [NOTE-2334](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2334.md). Within-person evidence, across 37 people, of the destabilization a tipping point predicts before entry into depression, in a minority of those who relapsed. Proposed until replicated in another sample; it is not evidence of hysteresis. | Proposed |
